items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A molecule or bond with a partial positive charge at one end and a partial negative charge at the other"?
items.answer: dipole
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of dipole.

items.stem: "Hydrogen bonds are the bonds that hold hydrogen and oxygen together inside a water molecule." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Inside a water molecule the bonds are polar covalent; hydrogen bonds are weaker attractions between δ+ hydrogen of one molecule and δ− oxygen of another molecule.
items.markingKey: Inside a water molecule the bonds are polar covalent; hydrogen bonds are weaker attractions between δ+ hydrogen of one molecule and δ− oxygen of another molecule. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why ice floats on liquid water and why this matters to aquatic organisms.
items.answer: In ice, hydrogen bonds hold each molecule in a fixed, open tetrahedral lattice, so ice is less dense than liquid water and floats; the surface ice insulates the water below, so it does not freeze solid and organisms survive the winter.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: In ice, hydrogen bonds hold each molecule in a fixed, open tetrahedral lattice, so ice is less dense than liquid water and floats; the surface ice insulates the water below, so it does not freeze solid and organisms survive the winter. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Ammonia, hydrogen fluoride and water all have unusually high boiling points for their molecular masses. What do they have in common?
options: Hydrogen bonded to a highly electronegative atom (N, F or O).
items.answer: Hydrogen bonded to a highly electronegative atom (N, F or O).
items.markingKey: C. Hydrogen bonding requires H attached to N, O or F.

items.stem: Using the survival of fish under the winter ice of Lake Baikal as an example, explain the effect of hydrogen bonding on the density of water.
items.answer: Ice up to a metre thick forms at the surface and floats, insulating the liquid water below, where temperatures stay near 4 °C. Hydrogen bonds fix molecules in an open lattice in ice, so ice is less dense than water, floats and insulates the habitat below.
items.markingKey: Context (Ice up to a metre thick forms at the surface and floats, insulating the liquid water below, where temperatures stay near 4 °C.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Hydrogen bonds fix molecules in an open lattice in ice, so ice is less dense than water, floats and insulates the habitat below. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the effect of hydrogen bonding on the density of water.

items.stem:
Kwame measured the height to which pond water rose in clean glass capillary tubes of different internal diameters at 20 °C. Each value is the mean of three readings.

Internal diameter / mm | Mean height of water / mm
0.5 | 57.3
1.0 | 28.8
1.5 | 19.7
2.0 | 14.9
3.0 | 9.6

(a) Describe the relationship between tube diameter and the height of water. [2]
(b) Calculate the percentage increase in height when the diameter is reduced from 1.0 mm to 0.5 mm. [2]
(c) Height × diameter is approximately constant. Use the data to predict the height of water in a tube of internal diameter 0.8 mm. [2]
items.answer: (a) As diameter increases the height decreases; halving the diameter roughly doubles the height (inverse proportion). (b) 99 % (c) ≈ 36.4 mm
items.markingKey: (a) [2] Height decreases as diameter increases (A1); idea of inverse proportionality / non-linear (A1). (b) [2] (57.3 − 28.8)/28.8 × 100 (M1) = 99 % (A1). (c) [2] Mean of h × d ≈ 29.1 mm² (M1); 29.1/0.8 = 36.4 mm (A1); accept ±5 %.

items.stem: Define the term "polar covalent bond".
items.answer: A covalent bond in which electrons are shared unequally because one atom is more electronegative, giving the atoms partial charges (δ+ and δ−)
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a covalent bond in which electrons are shared unequally because one atom is more electronegative, giving the atoms partial charges (δ+ and δ−). Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which molecule would NOT be expected to form hydrogen bonds with water?
items.answer: methane (CH₄)
items.markingKey: D. C–H bonds are almost non-polar, so methane has no δ+ H or δ− atom to bond with water.

items.stem: Distinguish between a hydrogen bond and a polar covalent bond.
items.answer: A polar covalent bond is a strong intramolecular bond in which electrons are shared unequally (e.g. O–H within water); a hydrogen bond is a weak intermolecular attraction between δ+ H of one molecule and δ− O/N of another.
items.markingKey: A polar covalent bond is a strong intramolecular bond in which electrons are shared unequally (e.g. O–H within water); a hydrogen bond is a weak intermolecular attraction between δ+ H of one molecule and δ− O/N of another. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Mei writes: "Hydrogen bonds are the bonds that hold hydrogen and oxygen together inside a water molecule." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Inside a water molecule the bonds are polar covalent; hydrogen bonds are weaker attractions between δ+ hydrogen of one molecule and δ− oxygen of another molecule.
items.markingKey: Inside a water molecule the bonds are polar covalent; hydrogen bonds are weaker attractions between δ+ hydrogen of one molecule and δ− oxygen of another molecule. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Felix supplied 5000 J of energy from an electric immersion heater to 200 g samples of water and of vegetable oil, each in an insulated beaker, and recorded the temperature rise.

Liquid | Mass / g | Energy supplied / J | Temperature rise / °C
water | 200 | 5000 | 5.9
vegetable oil | 200 | 5000 | 12.6

(a) State which liquid showed the greater temperature rise. [1]
(b) Calculate the specific heat capacity of each liquid in J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹, using c = Q/(m ΔT). [2]
(c) Calculate how many percent greater the specific heat capacity of water is than that of vegetable oil. [2]
items.answer: (a) vegetable oil (b) water 4.24; vegetable oil 1.98 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ (c) 114 %

items.stem: Predict, with a reason, whether ammonia (NH₃) can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.
items.answer: Yes: nitrogen is highly electronegative so N–H bonds are polar; the δ− N can attract δ+ H of water and the δ+ H of ammonia can attract δ− O of water.
items.markingKey: Yes: nitrogen is highly electronegative so N–H bonds are polar; the δ− N can attract δ+ H of water and the δ+ H of ammonia can attract δ− O of water.

items.stem: Outline the structure of a water molecule and explain how its polarity leads to hydrogen bonding and to two properties that are important for living organisms.
items.answer: Two H atoms covalently bonded to O; bent shape about 104.5°; O more electronegative so δ−, H δ+; molecule is a dipole; δ+ H attracts δ− O of another molecule = hydrogen bond; each molecule can form up to four; property 1 e.g. cohesion allowing transpiration pull in xylem; property 2 e.g. high specific heat capacity giving thermally stable habitats; or solvent for polar/ionic substances; or ice floating.
items.markingKey: Two H atoms covalently bonded to O; bent shape about 104.5°; O more electronegative so δ−, H δ+; molecule is a dipole; δ+ H attracts δ− O of another molecule = hydrogen bond; each molecule can form up to four; property 1 e.g. cohesion allowing transpiration pull in xylem; property 2 e.g. high specific heat capacity giving thermally stable habitats; or solvent for polar/ionic substances; or ice floating.

items.stem: "Hydrogen bonding is the single most important reason why water is suitable as the medium for life." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Hydrogen bonding underlies most of water’s life-supporting properties, but polarity more generally, and planetary conditions that keep water liquid, are also required; it is the most important single molecular property rather than the only factor.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: cohesion, adhesion, high specific heat capacity, high latent heat and the density anomaly of ice all arise from hydrogen bonding; hydrogen bonds with solutes allow polar molecules such as sugars and amino acids to dissolve. Arguments against: the polarity of water (attraction to ions) explains the solubility of salts without hydrogen bonds; other factors such as the liquid range at Earth temperatures and the abundance of water on Earth are also essential. Supported judgement: Hydrogen bonding underlies most of water’s life-supporting properties, but polarity more generally, and planetary conditions that keep water liquid, are also required; it is the most important single molecular property rather than the only factor. Markbands (8 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Define the term "adhesion".
items.answer: The attraction between molecules of different substances, such as water and the polar walls of xylem vessels
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the attraction between molecules of different substances, such as water and the polar walls of xylem vessels. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Why is oxygen carried in blood mainly by haemoglobin rather than dissolved in plasma?
options: Oxygen reacts with water to form an acid.
Oxygen molecules are too large to dissolve.
Oxygen is non-polar and has a low solubility in water.
items.answer: Oxygen is non-polar and has a low solubility in water.
items.markingKey: C. O₂ is non-polar; its solubility is far too low to meet metabolic demand.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain how cohesion and adhesion together allow water to move up xylem vessels.
items.answer: Evaporation from leaves creates tension; cohesion (hydrogen bonds between water molecules) transmits this tension down an unbroken column so water is pulled up; adhesion of water to the polar lignified/cellulose walls of xylem helps counter gravity and prevents the column breaking away from the walls. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Evaporation from leaves creates tension; cohesion (hydrogen bonds between water molecules) transmits this tension down an unbroken column so water is pulled up; adhesion of water to the polar lignified/cellulose walls of xylem helps counter gravity and prevents the column breaking away from the walls. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Soil water rises through narrow spaces between fine clay particles more than through coarse sand. Which property explains this?
options: capillary action due to adhesion and cohesion
items.answer: capillary action due to adhesion and cohesion
items.markingKey: D. Narrow spaces give stronger capillary rise.

items.stem: Predict how the following are transported in blood plasma, giving a reason for each: glucose, oxygen, sodium chloride, cholesterol.
items.answer: Glucose – dissolved (polar); oxygen – mostly bound to haemoglobin (non-polar, low solubility); NaCl – dissolved as Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions (ionic); cholesterol – in lipoproteins (hydrophobic).
items.markingKey: Glucose – dissolved (polar); oxygen – mostly bound to haemoglobin (non-polar, low solubility); NaCl – dissolved as Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions (ionic); cholesterol – in lipoproteins (hydrophobic).

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "The cohesion–tension theory fully explains how water reaches the tops of the tallest trees."
items.answer: Cohesion–tension is the main, well-supported mechanism, but a complete account must include adhesion, xylem structure that limits embolism, and minor contributions from root pressure.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: cohesion of water due to hydrogen bonding can sustain tensions large enough to lift water over 100 m; measured negative pressures in xylem and the narrowing of trunks during the day support the theory. Arguments against: air bubbles (cavitation/embolism) can break the column, so additional mechanisms such as refilling and parallel vessels are needed; root pressure can contribute in some plants, especially at night or in spring. Supported judgement: Cohesion–tension is the main, well-supported mechanism, but a complete account must include adhesion, xylem structure that limits embolism, and minor contributions from root pressure.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "surface tension"?
options: The tendency of the surface of a liquid to resist an external force, caused by cohesion between surface molecules
A molecule or bond with a partial positive charge at one end and a partial negative charge at the other
The tendency of an atom to attract the shared electrons of a covalent bond towards itself
The ratio of deuterium to ordinary hydrogen in a sample of water, used to trace the source of Earth’s water
items.answer: The tendency of the surface of a liquid to resist an external force, caused by cohesion between surface molecules
items.markingKey: A. "surface tension" is the tendency of the surface of a liquid to resist an external force, caused by cohesion between surface molecules.

items.stem: Distinguish between cohesion and adhesion.
items.answer: Cohesion is attraction between water molecules themselves (hydrogen bonds between water molecules); adhesion is attraction between water and a different polar or charged substance such as cellulose or glass.
items.markingKey: Cohesion is attraction between water molecules themselves (hydrogen bonds between water molecules); adhesion is attraction between water and a different polar or charged substance such as cellulose or glass. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Mateo writes: "Water moves up xylem because of adhesion alone." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Adhesion helps, but the main mechanism is cohesion–tension: transpiration creates tension that is transmitted down the column because water molecules are held together by cohesion.
items.markingKey: Adhesion helps, but the main mechanism is cohesion–tension: transpiration creates tension that is transmitted down the column because water molecules are held together by cohesion. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe the transport of water up a 100 m coast redwood (Sequoia sempervirens) and explain what it reveals about cohesion and adhesion in water transport.
items.answer: Water is pulled from roots to leaves through xylem, with tensions of several megapascals in the column. Cohesion keeps the column continuous under tension; adhesion to xylem walls supports it, allowing water to reach great heights without a pump.
items.markingKey: Context (Water is pulled from roots to leaves through xylem, with tensions of several megapascals in the column.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Cohesion keeps the column continuous under tension; adhesion to xylem walls supports it, allowing water to reach great heights without a pump. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to cohesion and adhesion in water transport.

items.stem: A student claims: "Water dissolves everything because it is the universal solvent." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Water dissolves polar and ionic substances; non-polar substances such as lipids are hydrophobic and do not dissolve.
items.markingKey: Water dissolves polar and ionic substances; non-polar substances such as lipids are hydrophobic and do not dissolve. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Lukas measured the height to which pond water rose in clean glass capillary tubes of different internal diameters at 20 °C. Each value is the mean of three readings.

Internal diameter / mm | Mean height of water / mm
0.5 | 60.3
1.0 | 28.9
1.5 | 19.4
2.0 | 14.6
3.0 | 9.3

(a) Describe the relationship between tube diameter and the height of water. [2]
(b) Calculate the percentage increase in height when the diameter is reduced from 1.0 mm to 0.5 mm. [2]
(c) Height × diameter is approximately constant. Use the data to predict the height of water in a tube of internal diameter 0.6 mm. [2]
(d) Explain, in terms of the properties of water, why water rises in a narrow glass tube. [3]
items.answer: (a) As diameter increases the height decreases; halving the diameter roughly doubles the height (inverse proportion). (b) 109 % (c) ≈ 48.4 mm (d) Adhesion of polar water molecules to the polar glass pulls water up the walls; cohesion (hydrogen bonds) pulls the rest of the column up behind; rise stops when the weight of the column balances these forces.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] Height decreases as diameter increases (A1); idea of inverse proportionality / non-linear (A1). (b) [2] (60.3 − 28.9)/28.9 × 100 (M1) = 109 % (A1). (c) [2] Mean of h × d ≈ 29.1 mm² (M1); 29.1/0.6 = 48.4 mm (A1); accept ±5 %. (d) [3] Adhesion to glass (A1); cohesion between water molecules/hydrogen bonds (A1); balance with weight of column / narrower tube = less mass per unit wall contact (A1).

items.stem: Describe how the cohesive, adhesive and solvent properties of water are each significant for living organisms. Use a named example for each property.
items.answer: Cohesion: hydrogen bonds between water molecules; allows transpiration pull in xylem / surface tension for pond skaters. Adhesion: water attracted to polar surfaces; capillary action in cell walls/xylem/soil. Solvent: polar water dissolves ions and polar molecules; e.g. glucose and amino acids transported in plasma, metabolic reactions in cytoplasm; non-polar substances such as cholesterol need carriers.
items.markingKey: Cohesion: hydrogen bonds between water molecules; allows transpiration pull in xylem / surface tension for pond skaters. Adhesion: water attracted to polar surfaces; capillary action in cell walls/xylem/soil. Solvent: polar water dissolves ions and polar molecules; e.g. glucose and amino acids transported in plasma, metabolic reactions in cytoplasm; non-polar substances such as cholesterol need carriers.

items.stem: Approximately what is the specific heat capacity of liquid water?
items.answer: 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹
items.markingKey: C. About 4.2 J are needed to raise 1 g of water by 1 °C.

items.stem: "Animals in water lose heat more slowly than in air because water is a stable habitat." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Water has a higher thermal conductivity than air, so animals in water lose heat faster; water’s temperature is stable, but heat loss from bodies is greater.
items.markingKey: Water has a higher thermal conductivity than air, so animals in water lose heat faster; water’s temperature is stable, but heat loss from bodies is greater. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why aquatic habitats have more stable temperatures than terrestrial habitats.
items.answer: Water has a high specific heat capacity, so it absorbs or loses a lot of energy for a small change in temperature; daily and seasonal fluctuations are therefore smaller in water.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Water has a high specific heat capacity, so it absorbs or loses a lot of energy for a small change in temperature; daily and seasonal fluctuations are therefore smaller in water. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe the ringed seal (Pusa hispida) and the black-throated loon (Gavia arctica) and explain what it reveals about how the physical properties of air and water differ for organisms.
items.answer: The seal is a streamlined swimmer insulated by blubber; the loon flies in air and dives in water, using feathers for insulation. Water’s higher density, viscosity and thermal conductivity favour streamlining and blubber in the seal, while the loon must cope with both media.
items.markingKey: Context (The seal is a streamlined swimmer insulated by blubber; the loon flies in air and dives in water, using feathers for insulation.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Water’s higher density, viscosity and thermal conductivity favour streamlining and blubber in the seal, while the loon must cope with both media. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how the physical properties of air and water differ for organisms.

items.stem: A cyclist in Dubai evaporates 750 g of sweat during a training ride. Taking the latent heat of vaporisation of water as 2.4 kJ g⁻¹, calculate the heat removed. Then calculate the mass of sweat that would need to evaporate to remove 1000 kJ, and explain why evaporation is such an effective cooling mechanism.
items.markingKey: 750 × 2.4 = 1800 kJ (A1); 1000/2.4 = 417 g (A1); many hydrogen bonds must be broken for each molecule to evaporate, so a lot of energy is absorbed from the surface (R1).

items.stem: Compare and contrast the physical properties of air and water as habitats, and explain how these properties have influenced the adaptations of a named aquatic mammal.
items.answer: Comparisons: water denser (buoyancy), more viscous (drag), higher thermal conductivity (heat loss), higher specific heat capacity (stable temperature); both are fluids that allow movement. Named mammal e.g. ringed seal: streamlined body reduces drag; thick blubber reduces heat loss by conduction; flippers for propulsion; buoyancy reduces skeletal load.
items.markingKey: Comparisons: water denser (buoyancy), more viscous (drag), higher thermal conductivity (heat loss), higher specific heat capacity (stable temperature); both are fluids that allow movement. Named mammal e.g. ringed seal: streamlined body reduces drag; thick blubber reduces heat loss by conduction; flippers for propulsion; buoyancy reduces skeletal load.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The ability of a substance to transfer heat energy through itself"?
items.answer: thermal conductivity
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of thermal conductivity.

items.stem: Distinguish between specific heat capacity and latent heat of vaporisation.
items.answer: Specific heat capacity is the energy to raise the temperature of a unit mass by 1 °C (no change of state); latent heat of vaporisation is the energy to change a unit mass of liquid to gas at constant temperature.
items.markingKey: Specific heat capacity is the energy to raise the temperature of a unit mass by 1 °C (no change of state); latent heat of vaporisation is the energy to change a unit mass of liquid to gas at constant temperature. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Which property of water makes it a more stable habitat than air for small organisms?
items.answer: its high specific heat capacity
items.markingKey: A. Water temperature changes slowly, reducing thermal stress.

items.stem: Coastal cities such as Lisbon have smaller annual temperature ranges than inland cities at the same latitude. Which property of water best explains this?
items.answer: high specific heat capacity
items.markingKey: A. The ocean absorbs and releases heat slowly, moderating the climate.

items.stem: A dog pants and evaporates 300 g of water from its respiratory surfaces in an hour on a hot day in Oslo. Taking the latent heat of vaporisation of water as 2.4 kJ g⁻¹, calculate the heat removed. Then calculate the mass of water that would need to evaporate to remove 3000 kJ, and explain why evaporation is such an effective cooling mechanism.
items.markingKey: 300 × 2.4 = 720 kJ (A1); 3000/2.4 = 1250 g (A1); many hydrogen bonds must be broken for each molecule to evaporate, so a lot of energy is absorbed from the surface (R1).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The thermal properties of water are more important to living organisms than its solvent properties."
items.answer: Solvent properties are more fundamental because they make metabolism possible; thermal properties are important for stability and regulation, so both matter but solvent properties are more essential.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: high specific heat capacity stabilises habitats and body temperature; evaporative cooling is essential for thermoregulation in many mammals and plants. Arguments against: without water acting as a solvent, metabolism and transport could not occur at all; many organisms survive large temperature changes but none can survive without aqueous cytoplasm. Supported judgement: Solvent properties are more fundamental because they make metabolism possible; thermal properties are important for stability and regulation, so both matter but solvent properties are more essential. items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "Goldilocks zone".
items.answer: The range of distances from a star (the habitable zone) at which a planet’s surface temperature allows liquid water to exist
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the range of distances from a star (the habitable zone) at which a planet’s surface temperature allows liquid water to exist. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Freya writes: "Water has always been on Earth because it formed from the same material as the planet in a hot state." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The early Earth was very hot and much water would have been lost; much of the present water is thought to have been delivered later by water-rich asteroids.
items.markingKey: The early Earth was very hot and much water would have been lost; much of the present water is thought to have been delivered later by water-rich asteroids. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to NASA’s Cassini mission flying through the plumes of Enceladus, explain how it illustrates the link between water and the search for extraterrestrial life.
items.answer: Cassini detected water, salts, silica and organic molecules in plumes erupting from a subsurface ocean. Evidence of liquid water with chemical energy makes Enceladus a prime target in the search for life.
items.markingKey: Context (Cassini detected water, salts, silica and organic molecules in plumes erupting from a subsurface ocean.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Evidence of liquid water with chemical energy makes Enceladus a prime target in the search for life. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the link between water and the search for extraterrestrial life.

items.stem: The D/H ratio of Earth’s ocean water is 1.56 × 10⁻⁴ and that of comet 103P/Hartley 2 is 1.61 × 10⁻⁴. How many times greater is the ratio for comet 103P/Hartley 2, and is it consistent with being a major source of Earth’s water?
items.answer: 1.03 times; consistent
items.markingKey: B. 1.61/1.56 = 1.03; a ratio close to 1 matches ocean water.

items.stem: Outline the hypotheses for the origin of water on Earth, and discuss how this knowledge is used in the search for extraterrestrial life.
items.answer: Early Earth hot – water lost/limited; water delivered by asteroids (carbonaceous chondrites) – D/H matches oceans; comets – most have higher D/H; water retained because Earth in Goldilocks zone, sufficient gravity and atmosphere; search for life targets bodies with liquid water (Mars past, Europa, Enceladus); habitable zones of exoplanets estimated from stellar luminosity; water necessary but not sufficient.
items.markingKey: Early Earth hot – water lost/limited; water delivered by asteroids (carbonaceous chondrites) – D/H matches oceans; comets – most have higher D/H; water retained because Earth in Goldilocks zone, sufficient gravity and atmosphere; search for life targets bodies with liquid water (Mars past, Europa, Enceladus); habitable zones of exoplanets estimated from stellar luminosity; water necessary but not sufficient.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The ratio of deuterium to ordinary hydrogen in a sample of water, used to trace the source of Earth’s water"?
items.answer: D/H ratio
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of D/H ratio.

items.stem: Explain how the D/H ratio of water is used to test hypotheses about the origin of Earth’s water.
items.answer: Different sources (comets, asteroids, solar nebula) have characteristic D/H ratios; if a source’s ratio matches that of ocean water it is a plausible main source; carbonaceous chondrites match closely whereas many comets have higher ratios.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Different sources (comets, asteroids, solar nebula) have characteristic D/H ratios; if a source’s ratio matches that of ocean water it is a plausible main source; carbonaceous chondrites match closely whereas many comets have higher ratios. items.stem: The habitable (Goldilocks) zone of the Sun lies between about 0.95 AU and 1.37 AU. The distance of the zone scales with the square root of a star’s luminosity. an F-type star has a luminosity 9.0 times that of the Sun. Calculate the inner and outer limits of its habitable zone.
items.answer: 2.85 AU to 4.11 AU

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The search for extraterrestrial life should focus only on planets and moons with liquid water."
items.answer: Water is a sensible first priority because it is the only solvent known to support life, but some effort should be kept for other possibilities, as our definition of life is based on a single example.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: all known life requires liquid water as a solvent; it narrows the search to the most promising targets such as Europa, Enceladus and Mars. Arguments against: life elsewhere might use a different solvent such as liquid methane (e.g. on Titan); focusing only on water could cause us to miss unfamiliar forms of life. Supported judgement: Water is a sensible first priority because it is the only solvent known to support life, but some effort should be kept for other possibilities, as our definition of life is based on a single example. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "dipole"?
options: A molecule or bond with a partial positive charge at one end and a partial negative charge at the other
A weak intermolecular attraction between a partially positive hydrogen atom of one polar molecule and a partially negative atom (such as oxygen or nitrogen) of another
The ratio of deuterium to ordinary hydrogen in a sample of water, used to trace the source of Earth’s water
The upward force exerted by a fluid on an object immersed in it, which depends on the density of the fluid
items.answer: A molecule or bond with a partial positive charge at one end and a partial negative charge at the other
items.markingKey: A. "dipole" is a molecule or bond with a partial positive charge at one end and a partial negative charge at the other.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A liquid in which other substances (solutes) dissolve to form a solution"?
items.answer: solvent
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of solvent.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "viscosity"?
options: A molecule or bond with a partial positive charge at one end and a partial negative charge at the other
The attraction between molecules of different substances, such as water and the polar walls of xylem vessels
The watery environment in which the chemical reactions of life take place and in which the first cells are thought to have arisen
The resistance of a fluid to flow; water has low viscosity compared with oils
items.answer: The resistance of a fluid to flow; water has low viscosity compared with oils
items.markingKey: D. "viscosity" is the resistance of a fluid to flow; water has low viscosity compared with oils.

items.stem: Mars lies at the outer edge of the habitable zone but has no stable surface liquid water today. Which factor most explains this?
options: Its thin atmosphere and low pressure mean water freezes or sublimes.
Its surface is made of water ice only.
It is closer to the Sun than Earth.
It has a thicker atmosphere than Venus.
items.answer: Its thin atmosphere and low pressure mean water freezes or sublimes.
items.markingKey: A. Low pressure prevents stable liquid water even where temperatures allow.

items.stem: Explain the difference between hydrophilic substances and hydrophobic substances.
items.answer: Hydrophilic substances are polar or charged and are attracted to (dissolve in) water; hydrophobic substances are non-polar, cannot form hydrogen bonds with water and so do not dissolve, clustering together instead.
items.markingKey: Hydrophilic substances are polar or charged and are attracted to (dissolve in) water; hydrophobic substances are non-polar, cannot form hydrogen bonds with water and so do not dissolve, clustering together instead. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why sodium chloride and glucose are transported dissolved in blood plasma whereas cholesterol and fats are not.
items.answer: NaCl is ionic and glucose is polar, so both are attracted to water and dissolve; cholesterol and fats are non-polar/hydrophobic, so they are carried in lipoprotein particles with a hydrophilic outer layer of phospholipids and proteins.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: NaCl is ionic and glucose is polar, so both are attracted to water and dissolve; cholesterol and fats are non-polar/hydrophobic, so they are carried in lipoprotein particles with a hydrophilic outer layer of phospholipids and proteins. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Why does a ringed seal need thick blubber whereas an Arctic bird such as a loon relies mainly on feathers?
options: Water conducts heat away about 25 times faster than air, so animals in water lose heat more rapidly.
Air has a higher specific heat capacity.
Feathers do not work in cold air.
items.answer: Water conducts heat away about 25 times faster than air, so animals in water lose heat more rapidly.
items.markingKey: B. High thermal conductivity of water makes insulation critical.

items.stem: Distinguish between the asteroid hypothesis and the comet hypothesis for the origin of Earth’s water.
items.answer: The asteroid hypothesis proposes water-rich carbonaceous asteroids delivered most water, supported by their Earth-like D/H ratio; the comet hypothesis proposes icy comets, but most measured comets (e.g. 67P) have D/H ratios much higher than Earth’s oceans.
items.markingKey: The asteroid hypothesis proposes water-rich carbonaceous asteroids delivered most water, supported by their Earth-like D/H ratio; the comet hypothesis proposes icy comets, but most measured comets (e.g. 67P) have D/H ratios much higher than Earth’s oceans. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why is ice less dense than liquid water at 0 °C?
options: Molecules in ice have lost hydrogen atoms.
Covalent bonds lengthen when water freezes.
Hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open lattice with larger spaces between them.
Ice contains trapped bubbles of air.
items.answer: Hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open lattice with larger spaces between them.
items.markingKey: C. In ice each molecule is fixed in a tetrahedral, hydrogen-bonded lattice that is more open than the liquid.

items.stem:
Ana measured the height to which pond water rose in clean glass capillary tubes of different internal diameters at 20 °C. Each value is the mean of three readings.

Internal diameter / mm | Mean height of water / mm
0.5 | 60.3
1.0 | 31.1
1.5 | 20.8
2.0 | 15.5
3.0 | 10.1

(a) Describe the relationship between tube diameter and the height of water. [2]
(b) Calculate the percentage increase in height when the diameter is reduced from 1.0 mm to 0.5 mm. [2]
items.answer: (a) As diameter increases the height decreases; halving the diameter roughly doubles the height (inverse proportion). (b) 94 %
items.markingKey: (a) [2] Height decreases as diameter increases (A1); idea of inverse proportionality / non-linear (A1). (b) [2] (60.3 − 31.1)/31.1 × 100 (M1) = 94 % (A1).

items.stem: Isabel writes: "Sweating cools you because the sweat itself is cold." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Sweat is at body temperature; cooling occurs because evaporation absorbs a large amount of heat energy (high latent heat of vaporisation) from the skin.
items.markingKey: Sweat is at body temperature; cooling occurs because evaporation absorbs a large amount of heat energy (high latent heat of vaporisation) from the skin. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Water vapour plumes from Saturn’s moon Enceladus contain salts, silica and simple organic molecules. Why does this make Enceladus a target for astrobiology?
options: It shows the water came from Earth.
It proves life exists on Enceladus.
It suggests a liquid water ocean in contact with rock, a possible energy and chemical source for life.
It shows Enceladus is in the Sun’s habitable zone.
items.answer: It suggests a liquid water ocean in contact with rock, a possible energy and chemical source for life.
items.markingKey: C. Liquid water plus energy plus chemistry are the requirements for life as we know it.

items.stem: Briefly describe hydrothermal vents on the floor of the Atlantic Ocean and explain what it reveals about water as the medium for life.
items.answer: Mineral-rich water at vents provides a liquid medium in which chemical energy gradients exist, a proposed site for the origin of life. Water dissolves the reactants (ions, small polar molecules) and allows them to collide and react, so it is a plausible medium for the first metabolism.
items.markingKey: Context (Mineral-rich water at vents provides a liquid medium in which chemical energy gradients exist, a proposed site for the origin of life.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Water dissolves the reactants (ions, small polar molecules) and allows them to collide and react, so it is a plausible medium for the first metabolism. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to water as the medium for life.

items.stem: A paper towel dipped in water draws water upwards several centimetres. Explain this observation using two properties of water.
items.answer: Adhesion between water and the polar cellulose fibres pulls water along the fibres; cohesion between water molecules draws more water up behind = capillary action.
items.markingKey: Adhesion between water and the polar cellulose fibres pulls water along the fibres; cohesion between water molecules draws more water up behind = capillary action.

items.stem:
Amara supplied 8000 J of energy from an electric immersion heater to 50 g samples of water and of seawater, each in an insulated beaker, and recorded the temperature rise.

Liquid | Mass / g | Energy supplied / J | Temperature rise / °C
water | 50 | 8000 | 38.2
seawater | 50 | 8000 | 40.0

(a) State which liquid showed the greater temperature rise. [1]
(b) Calculate the specific heat capacity of each liquid in J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹, using c = Q/(m ΔT). [2]
(c) Calculate how many percent greater the specific heat capacity of water is than that of seawater. [2]
items.answer: (a) seawater (b) water 4.19; seawater 4.00 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ (c) 5 %

items.stem: A star has a luminosity 4 times that of the Sun. The Sun’s habitable zone lies about 0.95–1.37 AU from it. Where would the habitable zone of this star lie?
items.answer: about 1.9–2.7 AU
items.markingKey: A. Distance scales with √L: √4 = 2, so 1.9–2.7 AU.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Hydrogen bonding is the single most important reason why water is suitable as the medium for life."
items.answer: Hydrogen bonding underlies most of water’s life-supporting properties, but polarity more generally, and planetary conditions that keep water liquid, are also required; it is the most important single molecular property rather than the only factor.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: cohesion, adhesion, high specific heat capacity, high latent heat and the density anomaly of ice all arise from hydrogen bonding; hydrogen bonds with solutes allow polar molecules such as sugars and amino acids to dissolve. Arguments against: the polarity of water (attraction to ions) explains the solubility of salts without hydrogen bonds; other factors such as the liquid range at Earth temperatures and the abundance of water on Earth are also essential. Supported judgement: Hydrogen bonding underlies most of water’s life-supporting properties, but polarity more generally, and planetary conditions that keep water liquid, are also required; it is the most important single molecular property rather than the only factor.

items.stem: "The cohesion–tension theory fully explains how water reaches the tops of the tallest trees." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Cohesion–tension is the main, well-supported mechanism, but a complete account must include adhesion, xylem structure that limits embolism, and minor contributions from root pressure.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: cohesion of water due to hydrogen bonding can sustain tensions large enough to lift water over 100 m; measured negative pressures in xylem and the narrowing of trunks during the day support the theory. Arguments against: air bubbles (cavitation/embolism) can break the column, so additional mechanisms such as refilling and parallel vessels are needed; root pressure can contribute in some plants, especially at night or in spring. Supported judgement: Cohesion–tension is the main, well-supported mechanism, but a complete account must include adhesion, xylem structure that limits embolism, and minor contributions from root pressure. items.stem:
Ana supplied 6000 J of energy from an electric immersion heater to 50 g samples of water and of glycerol, each in an insulated beaker, and recorded the temperature rise.

Liquid | Mass / g | Energy supplied / J | Temperature rise / °C
water | 50 | 6000 | 28.6
glycerol | 50 | 6000 | 49.9

(a) State which liquid showed the greater temperature rise. [1]
(b) Calculate the specific heat capacity of each liquid in J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹, using c = Q/(m ΔT). [2]
(c) Calculate how many percent greater the specific heat capacity of water is than that of glycerol. [2]
(d) Explain why water has a high specific heat capacity. [2]
items.answer: (a) glycerol (b) water 4.20; glycerol 2.40 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ (c) 74 % (d) Much of the energy supplied is used to break the many hydrogen bonds between water molecules rather than increasing their kinetic energy.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] glycerol (A1). (b) [2] Water: 6000/(50 × 28.6) = 4.20 (A1); glycerol: 6000/(50 × 49.9) = 2.40 (A1). (c) [2] (4.20 − 2.40)/2.40 × 100 (M1) = 74 % (A1). (d) [2] Hydrogen bonds between molecules (A1); energy used to break them before temperature rises (A1).

items.stem: "The search for extraterrestrial life should focus only on planets and moons with liquid water." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Water is a sensible first priority because it is the only solvent known to support life, but some effort should be kept for other possibilities, as our definition of life is based on a single example.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: all known life requires liquid water as a solvent; it narrows the search to the most promising targets such as Europa, Enceladus and Mars. Arguments against: life elsewhere might use a different solvent such as liquid methane (e.g. on Titan); focusing only on water could cause us to miss unfamiliar forms of life. Supported judgement: Water is a sensible first priority because it is the only solvent known to support life, but some effort should be kept for other possibilities, as our definition of life is based on a single example. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Which feature of the water molecule, together with unequal electron sharing, makes the whole molecule polar?
items.answer: its bent (V-shaped) geometry
items.markingKey: B. The bent shape (about 104.5°) means the bond dipoles do not cancel.

items.stem: Which property of water allows a pond skater (Gerris) to walk on the surface of a pond?
options: adhesion of water to the insect’s legs
the high specific heat capacity of water
items.answer: surface tension resulting from cohesion
items.markingKey: A. Cohesion between surface water molecules produces surface tension that supports the insect.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "latent heat of vaporisation".
items.answer: The energy required to convert a liquid into vapour without a change in temperature; for water it is very high because hydrogen bonds must be broken
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the energy required to convert a liquid into vapour without a change in temperature; for water it is very high because hydrogen bonds must be broken. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Comet 67P has a D/H ratio about three times that of Earth’s oceans. What does this suggest?
options: All of Earth’s water came from 67P-type comets.
Comets similar to 67P were not the main source of Earth’s water.
Earth’s water formed from the Sun.
items.answer: Comets similar to 67P were not the main source of Earth’s water.
items.markingKey: C. A mismatch in D/H ratio argues against that source.

items.stem: Explain why water has a much higher boiling point than other molecules of similar size, such as methane.
items.answer: Extensive hydrogen bonding between polar water molecules means much energy is needed to separate them into vapour; methane is non-polar with only weak intermolecular forces.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Extensive hydrogen bonding between polar water molecules means much energy is needed to separate them into vapour; methane is non-polar with only weak intermolecular forces. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Which is an example of adhesion rather than cohesion?
options: a water strider standing on a pond surface
a column of water held together in a xylem vessel
water forming spherical droplets on a waxy leaf
water moving through the cellulose cell walls of a leaf
items.answer: water moving through the cellulose cell walls of a leaf
items.markingKey: D. Cellulose is polar; water adheres to it.

items.stem: Explain the difference between water and air as a medium for animals.
items.answer: Water has higher density, viscosity, buoyancy, thermal conductivity and specific heat capacity than air: aquatic animals are supported but face drag and faster heat loss; animals in air need skeletal support or lift but lose heat more slowly.
items.markingKey: Water has higher density, viscosity, buoyancy, thermal conductivity and specific heat capacity than air: aquatic animals are supported but face drag and faster heat loss; animals in air need skeletal support or lift but lose heat more slowly. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Amara writes: "If a planet has water, it must have life." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Liquid water is a necessary condition for life as we know it, but not a sufficient one; energy sources, suitable chemistry and time are also needed.
items.markingKey: Liquid water is a necessary condition for life as we know it, but not a sufficient one; energy sources, suitable chemistry and time are also needed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a polar covalent bond and a hydrogen bond.
items.answer: A polar covalent bond is a strong intramolecular bond in which electrons are shared unequally (e.g. O–H within water); a hydrogen bond is a weak intermolecular attraction between δ+ H of one molecule and δ− O/N of another.
items.markingKey: A polar covalent bond is a strong intramolecular bond in which electrons are shared unequally (e.g. O–H within water); a hydrogen bond is a weak intermolecular attraction between δ+ H of one molecule and δ− O/N of another. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With reference to pond skaters (Gerris lacustris) moving across the surface of a pond, explain how it illustrates surface tension.
items.answer: The insects stand on the water surface without breaking it, spreading their weight on hydrophobic hairy legs. Cohesion between surface water molecules creates a film strong enough to support small animals.
items.markingKey: Context (The insects stand on the water surface without breaking it, spreading their weight on hydrophobic hairy legs.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Cohesion between surface water molecules creates a film strong enough to support small animals. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to surface tension.

items.stem: A 70 kg runner loses 500 g of sweat by evaporation during a race. Taking the latent heat of vaporisation of water as 2.4 kJ g⁻¹, how much heat is removed?

The D/H ratio of Earth’s ocean water is 1.56 × 10⁻⁴ and that of comet 46P/Wirtanen is 1.61 × 10⁻⁴. How many times greater is the ratio for comet 46P/Wirtanen, and is it consistent with being a major source of Earth’s water?
items.answer: 1.03 times; consistent
items.markingKey: D. 1.61/1.56 = 1.03; a ratio close to 1 matches ocean water.

items.stem: A lake in Finland freezes over in winter, yet fish survive. Which explanation links this to the structure of water?
options: Ice sinks and protects the fish from predators.
Fish produce heat that prevents the lake from freezing.
Ice floats because hydrogen bonds form an open lattice, and the floating ice insulates the liquid water beneath.
Liquid water is less dense than ice, so it rises to the top.
items.answer: Ice floats because hydrogen bonds form an open lattice, and the floating ice insulates the liquid water beneath.
items.markingKey: C. Floating ice insulates; the densest water (about 4 °C) collects at the bottom.

items.stem: A student claims: "Oxygen dissolves easily in blood plasma, which is why we have plasma." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Oxygen is non-polar and poorly soluble in water; most oxygen is carried bound to haemoglobin in red blood cells.
items.markingKey: Oxygen is non-polar and poorly soluble in water; most oxygen is carried bound to haemoglobin in red blood cells. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A cyclist in Kuala Lumpur evaporates 400 g of sweat during a training ride. Taking the latent heat of vaporisation of water as 2.4 kJ g⁻¹, calculate the heat removed. Then calculate the mass of sweat that would need to evaporate to remove 2500 kJ, and explain why evaporation is such an effective cooling mechanism.
items.markingKey: 400 × 2.4 = 960 kJ (A1); 2500/2.4 = 1042 g (A1); many hydrogen bonds must be broken for each molecule to evaporate, so a lot of energy is absorbed from the surface (R1).

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Rosetta mission’s measurements of comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko shows the testing of hypotheses about the origin of Earth’s water.
items.answer: Rosetta found a D/H ratio of about 5.3 × 10⁻⁴, over three times that of Earth’s oceans (about 1.56 × 10⁻⁴). The mismatch suggests comets like 67P were not the main source, supporting the asteroid hypothesis instead.
items.markingKey: Context (Rosetta found a D/H ratio of about 5.3 × 10⁻⁴, over three times that of Earth’s oceans (about 1.56 × 10⁻⁴).) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The mismatch suggests comets like 67P were not the main source, supporting the asteroid hypothesis instead. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the testing of hypotheses about the origin of Earth’s water.

items.stem:
Tariq supplied 5000 J of energy from an electric immersion heater to 50 g samples of water and of olive oil, each in an insulated beaker, and recorded the temperature rise.

Liquid | Mass / g | Energy supplied / J | Temperature rise / °C
water | 50 | 5000 | 23.3
olive oil | 50 | 5000 | 51.7

(a) State which liquid showed the greater temperature rise. [1]
(b) Calculate the specific heat capacity of each liquid in J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹, using c = Q/(m ΔT). [2]
(c) Calculate how many percent greater the specific heat capacity of water is than that of olive oil. [2]
(d) Explain why water has a high specific heat capacity. [2]
items.answer: (a) olive oil (b) water 4.29; olive oil 1.93 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ (c) 122 % (d) Much of the energy supplied is used to break the many hydrogen bonds between water molecules rather than increasing their kinetic energy.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] olive oil (A1). (b) [2] Water: 5000/(50 × 23.3) = 4.29 (A1); olive oil: 5000/(50 × 51.7) = 1.93 (A1). (c) [2] (4.29 − 1.93)/1.93 × 100 (M1) = 122 % (A1). (d) [2] Hydrogen bonds between molecules (A1); energy used to break them before temperature rises (A1).

items.stem:
Priya measured the height to which distilled water rose in clean glass capillary tubes of different internal diameters at 20 °C. Each value is the mean of three readings.

Internal diameter / mm | Mean height of water / mm
0.5 | 59.9
1.0 | 30.2
1.5 | 19.0
2.0 | 14.2
3.0 | 9.7

(a) Describe the relationship between tube diameter and the height of water. [2]
(b) Calculate the percentage increase in height when the diameter is reduced from 1.0 mm to 0.5 mm. [2]
(c) Height × diameter is approximately constant. Use the data to predict the height of water in a tube of internal diameter 0.8 mm. [2]
(d) Explain, in terms of the properties of water, why water rises in a narrow glass tube. [3]
(e) State one variable, other than temperature, that should be controlled. [1]
(f) Suggest how these results relate to water transport in plants. [2]
(g) Outline why each value was the mean of three readings. [1]
items.answer: (a) As diameter increases the height decreases; halving the diameter roughly doubles the height (inverse proportion). (b) 98 % (c) ≈ 36.5 mm (d) Adhesion of polar water molecules to the polar glass pulls water up the walls; cohesion (hydrogen bonds) pulls the rest of the column up behind; rise stops when the weight of the column balances these forces. (e) e.g. cleanliness/material of the tubes; type/purity of water; depth to which the tube is dipped. (f) Xylem vessels are narrow tubes with polar (lignified/cellulose) walls; capillary action contributes to water rise, but only by a small height, so transpiration pull is needed for tall plants. (g) Repeats allow anomalies to be identified and reduce the effect of random error, increasing reliability.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] Height decreases as diameter increases (A1); idea of inverse proportionality / non-linear (A1). (b) [2] (59.9 − 30.2)/30.2 × 100 (M1) = 98 % (A1). (c) [2] Mean of h × d ≈ 29.2 mm² (M1); 29.2/0.8 = 36.5 mm (A1); accept ±5 %. (d) [3] Adhesion to glass (A1); cohesion between water molecules/hydrogen bonds (A1); balance with weight of column / narrower tube = less mass per unit wall contact (A1). (e) [1] Any one valid controlled variable (A1). (f) [2] Xylem as narrow tubes with adhesive walls (A1); capillarity alone only lifts water a few cm / cohesion–tension needed for tall trees (R1). (g) [1] Reduce random error / identify anomalies (A1).
